volumes.title: The Empty Twelfth Plate
volumes.text:
My grandfather Fenwick Orrell painted signs on Tallow Lane in Emberwick, and on his free days he painted clouds. His catalogue has twelve plates. Eleven are finished. The twelfth is an empty ruled frame with one pencil line beneath it: Night-shiner. Seen once, midsummer, due north, past midnight. Not believed.

I am Tamsin Orrell, and the shop, the brushes and the catalogue are mine now. This July I have resolved to stand under each of his clouds in turn, a month apiece, and to fill that frame if the sky allows.

Plate one is the easy one, the bread-loaf cloud: flat grey base, white domed top, a whole bakery of them drifting over the Lowlands by noon. They rise where the warm fields breathe upward, and they flatten and vanish by evening. Fair weather. I ate my lunch under forty of them.

volumes.title: The Anvil over Harrow Fell
volumes.text:
August in Emberwick, and plate two of my grandfather's cloud catalogue: the anvil. I am Tamsin Orrell, sign painter of Tallow Lane, working through his eleven painted clouds toward the twelfth he never finished.

The anvil begins as an ordinary bread-loaf cloud that refuses to stop. By two o'clock it had heaped itself higher than Harrow Fell; by three its top had struck some ceiling in the air and spread flat, exactly like the smith's anvil on Cooper Street. Underneath, it went the colour of a ripe plum.

I counted from flash to thunder, five slow counts to the mile, as Grandfather taught me. Fifteen, then ten, then four. At four I carried my easel indoors. The hail that followed rattled the shop sign and was over in six minutes. His plate shows lilac in the shadow. He was right; I had always thought it fanciful.

volumes.title: Mare's Tails
volumes.text:
September. From the flat roof of the sign shop on Tallow Lane I can see the whole western sky, and this morning it was combed. Long white wisps, each hooked at one end like a hair caught on a brush, streamed in from the Grey Coast far above every other cloud. These are mare's tails, plate three in my grandfather Fenwick Orrell's catalogue, which I am following through the year.

They are made of ice, he wrote, and they sit so high that the wind up there has nothing to do with the wind down here. Beneath the plate is a rule in his square hand: rain in a day and a half.

I put it to the test with the shop clock. The first drops struck the skylight thirty-one hours later. I painted the tails as he did, with a nearly dry brush dragged once and never touched again.

volumes.title: A Cloud Sat Down
volumes.text:
My grandfather counted fog as a cloud, plate four of his catalogue, on the grounds that a cloud which has sat down is a cloud all the same. So in October I, Tamsin Orrell, left my sign shop in Emberwick before dawn and walked out along the marsh causeway to stand inside one.

There is nothing to see from within. That is the lesson. The world shrank to twenty paces of wet planks, a heron's complaint, and beads of water gathering on my sleeve and eyelashes. Fog is made of drops too small to fall.

Then I climbed the ladder of the old drainage mill and came out above it. The fog lay flat and white as a lake to the horizon, with the mill's sails and three poplars standing up out of it. By ten the sun had burned it to rags. I drew fast.

volumes.title: The Slate Sheet
volumes.text:
November's cloud is the one nobody loves. Plate five in the catalogue left to me by my grandfather, Fenwick Orrell, is a plain grey rectangle with one Emberwick chimney at the bottom for scale. He called it the slate sheet: a low, even layer with no edges, no towers and no intentions, which sat over Tallow Lane for nine days running.

I nearly skipped it. A sign painter likes a shape. But I had promised myself every plate, so I took my stool to the roof and looked properly.

It is not one grey. There is a pearl patch where the sun stands behind it, a darker band toward the fells whose tops it had swallowed, and a slow grain like brushed wool. It gives drizzle, never real rain. On the ninth day I mixed eleven greys before I was satisfied, and I felt oddly fond of it.

volumes.title: The Rain-Bearer
volumes.text:
Plate six of my grandfather's cloud catalogue is spotted, and for years I took the spots for mildew. They are rain. He painted the rain-bearer out of doors, and it rained on him.

I am Tamsin Orrell of Tallow Lane, Emberwick, and in December I did the same. The rain-bearer is thicker and darker than the slate sheet of last month, a deep wet ceiling with a ragged underside, and it means a whole day of weather. The lamps in the shop were lit at noon. Shreds of lower cloud hurried beneath it like late clerks.

At three the rain turned quiet, and I looked up to find it had become snow. I caught flakes on my dark sleeve: six points, every one, no two the same. My own plate has spots on it now. I have decided to leave them.

volumes.title: The Veil and the Ring
volumes.text:
January, clear and bitter, and then on the fourteenth the stars over Emberwick went soft. A thin milky veil had drawn across the whole sky, so fine that the moon shone through it and cast shadows. Around the moon stood a pale ring.

This is plate seven of the catalogue my grandfather Fenwick Orrell began and I, his granddaughter Tamsin, am finishing. The veil is ice, like mare's tails, but spread into a sheet. The ring is the moonlight bent through it. I measured it from the shop roof: one outstretched hand, thumb to little finger, from the moon to the ring, all the way round.

His note says: ring round the moon, snow by the second morning. It came by the first evening, four inches of it. The veil is honest, I find, but it does not keep exact appointments.

volumes.title: Harrow Fell Wears a Hat
volumes.text:
For plate eight I had to leave Emberwick. My grandfather's cloud catalogue shows a smooth white lens poised above a mountain, and that cloud, the hat, forms only where a strong wind is made to climb. So in February I rode the carrier's cart north to Fellfoot with my paintbox on my knees.

It was there when I arrived, sitting a little above the summit of Harrow Fell like a lid lifted off a pot. A gale was blowing. The hat did not move. I watched for two hours and understood at last: the wind pours through it, and the cloud is forever being made at the front edge and unmade at the back.

A shepherd stopped beside my easel. When Harrow wears his hat, he said, tie your own on. Mine was already in the beck. I, Tamsin Orrell, painted bareheaded.

volumes.title: Fish-Scale Sky
volumes.text:
On the Grey Coast they call it a herring sky. My grandfather, Fenwick Orrell, called it fish-scale and made it plate nine of his catalogue of clouds: hundreds of tiny white ripples, very high, laid in rows as neat as the flank of a fish. I am his granddaughter Tamsin, and I saw it in March from the harbour wall at Skerry Point, where I had gone to repaint a chandler's sign.

Each scale is smaller than my little fingernail held at arm's length. That is the test; anything bigger is another cloud altogether.

It does not last. Within the hour the rows had blurred and thickened. A woman gutting fish beside me said scales mean a change of wind and nothing settled, not long wet and not long dry. I dabbed mine in with the tip of one finger, which is how Grandfather did his. The prints are there.

volumes.title: The Dairy
volumes.text:
Plate ten is the rare one among the finished eleven. My grandfather called it the dairy. In his catalogue of clouds it carries a note: wait behind the storm, face east, be quick.

I am Tamsin Orrell, sign painter of Emberwick, and I waited all April. On the twenty-sixth a thunderstorm crossed the town at teatime and rumbled off toward the Lowlands. I ran up to the shop roof and faced east as instructed.

The underside of the storm's great shelf had let down pouches, dozens of them, round and soft as a row of udders. The low sun behind me lit each one gold with a bruise-blue shadow. Nothing I have painted on a signboard is as strange. They lasted eleven minutes by the church clock. Nine months of clouds had taught me speed, and I needed all of it. The paint was still wet when they smoothed away.

volumes.title: The Flock
volumes.text:
May over Emberwick, and plate eleven: the flock. It is a sheet of rounded white tufts with blue lanes between, drifting together at a middling height like sheep let out onto a hill. Each tuft is about the width of my thumb at arm's length, far larger than the fish-scales of March. At sunset they are lit from beneath, and the whole flock turns pink at once.

That completes the eleven clouds my grandfather Fenwick Orrell painted. I have stood under every one. There remains the twelfth frame, empty, and his pencil note: Night-shiner. Seen once, midsummer, due north, past midnight. Not believed.

So I, Tamsin, have changed my hours. I sleep after dinner and climb to the roof at eleven with a flask and a blanket. The nights are short and never fully dark now. North is a row of chimneys and a pale glow. Nothing yet.

volumes.title: The Night-Shiner
volumes.text:
Twelve nights I sat on the roof of the sign shop on Tallow Lane, facing north over the Emberwick chimneys. On the thirteenth, the twenty-first of June, at ten minutes to one, it came. Low in the north, where the midsummer glow never quite leaves, a web of fine ripples was shining silver-blue. Ordinary clouds are black at that hour. These were bright, because they float so far above all the others that the sun, well below the edge of the world, still reaches them.

My grandfather saw this once and was not believed. So I ran down and fetched Mr Pell the baker, who was already up with his dough. He stood a long while with flour on his arms and then signed my page as witness.

The twelfth plate is painted. Under Fenwick Orrell's pencil line his granddaughter Tamsin has added three words: Seen again. Believed.

volumes.title: The Wager at Skerry Point
volumes.text:
I am Maren Coldwick, signal-keeper at Skerry Point on the Grey Coast. When a gale is coming I hoist a black canvas cone on the mast so that the eleven boats of the fleet stay in. This September the town council sent me a new barometer, a handsome glass in a brass case, and old Jory Pike laughed at it.

Jory fished here for fifty years. He says he can smell a storm, and the gulls tell him the rest. So we have a wager, with Mrs Furze the harbourmaster as judge: a point for each storm called before it strikes, from now until spring. The loser paints the signal mast. The winner eats a herring supper at the loser's expense.

First blood to the glass. It fell all Monday; Jory said fair. On Tuesday the wind took every sheet off every washing line in the village.

volumes.title: Thunder from the Land
volumes.text:
Skerry Point, late September. Storm the second of the season came from the wrong direction entirely, and it has cost my barometer its lead.

The afternoon was hot and still. The glass in its brass case had not moved a hair since breakfast, and I, Maren Coldwick, signal-keeper, told Jory Pike so. He was sitting on an upturned crab pot, sniffing. Thunder by four, he said. The cows on the cliff field were all lying down, the gulls had gone quiet, and the air smelled of pennies.

At ten to four a cloud like a black cliff came over the hill from inland. Lightning struck the sea twice beyond the harbour bar. Rain fell so hard it bounced knee-high off the quay, and in half an hour the sun was out again. Mrs Furze, who judges our wager, has entered it in the book. One point each. Jory is unbearable.

volumes.title: The Equinox Gale
volumes.text:
The third storm of our wager needed no cleverness from anybody. I am Maren Coldwick, keeper of the signal mast at Skerry Point, matching my new barometer against Jory Pike's nose, and this time both were right.

The glass began to sink on Thursday noon and kept sinking. Jory came up the path at two to say the gulls were walking about in the turnip field like hens. I hoisted the black cone at three. All eleven boats stayed on their moorings.

It blew from the south-west for a night and a day. Spray came clean over the harbour wall and salted my windows on the landward side. Old hands call it the equinox gale and expect it yearly, as one expects an aunt. Mrs Furze, our judge, awards a point each. Two all. The mast still wants painting, and neither of us intends to do it.

volumes.title: Swell without Wind
volumes.text:
October at Skerry Point, flat calm and thick fog, and the barometer steady as a church. I am Maren Coldwick, signal-keeper, and I told Jory Pike there was nothing to call.

He stood on the quay with his head on one side, listening. The sea is breathing long, he said. Sure enough, between the small slaps of the harbour water there came, every quarter minute, a slow heavy heave against the outer wall. A storm was out there, hundreds of miles off, and had sent its swell ahead like a calling card.

No wind ever reached us. But by evening great smooth hills of water were rolling through the fog, and they smashed nine lobster pots on the skerries. Mrs Furze, who judges our wager, ruled that a storm you can hear counts as a storm. Jory three, the glass two. I have learned to listen for the long breath.

volumes.title: The Glass Is Avenged
volumes.text:
Storm the fifth, the second week of November, and a good day for brass and mercury. I keep the signal mast at Skerry Point on the Grey Coast; my name is Maren Coldwick; and for once Jory Pike was plainly, splendidly wrong.

The morning was bright. Gulls bobbed on the water like bath toys, which Jory holds to be a certain sign of settled weather. He told the whole quay the boats might go out. But my barometer had dropped three tenths of an inch between supper and breakfast, faster than I had yet seen it fall, and I hoisted the cone anyway.

The fleet grumbled and stayed. By two o'clock a south-westerly was tearing slates off the net loft. Jory watched from my window with a mug of tea and said the gulls had deceived him personally. Mrs Furze marked the wager book: three all.

volumes.title: A Cone for Nothing
volumes.text:
I am Maren Coldwick, signal-keeper at Skerry Point, and this page is a confession. In late November my barometer fell steeply, just as it had before the last gale. I hoisted the black cone. Eleven boats stayed in harbour on what should have been the best herring day of the month.

Nothing came. It rained, gently, straight down. A child could have sailed a washtub to the skerries and back. Jory Pike had said so at dawn: the gulls were far out at sea and his knee was quiet.

I have since learned that the glass falls for rain as well as wind, and that it is the speed of the fall, together with the sky, that tells them apart. Mrs Furze ruled that a false alarm hands the point to the other side. Jory four, glass three. The fleet forgave me by Thursday. Jory has not stopped smiling yet.

volumes.title: Snow from the North
volumes.text:
December on the Grey Coast. The seventh storm of the season came down from the Northern Fells instead of in from the sea, and it came white.

Two nights earlier Jory Pike had pointed out a ring around the moon, and that afternoon he showed me geese flying south very low and in a hurry. My barometer agreed with him for once, falling slowly and steadily for a day and a half. I, Maren Coldwick, hoisted the cone at Skerry Point with stiff fingers, and we were both right.

The wind swung north and the snow drove sideways for nine hours. In the morning the boats wore white caps, the mast had a drift up its windward side, and the harbour was skinned with slush that rose and fell like porridge. Our judge, Mrs Furze, gave a point each. Jory five, glass four. We dug out her door together.

volumes.title: The Glazed Mast
volumes.text:
Neither of us called the eighth storm, and I record it for honesty's sake. I am Maren Coldwick, signal-keeper at Skerry Point, and I have a wager running between my barometer and old Jory Pike's weather sense.

On a still January night rain fell through freezing air and froze where it landed. There was no wind and scarcely a movement of the glass. Jory's gulls gave no sign. We woke to a village dipped in clear ice: every rope, every rung, every blade of grass on the cliff. The signal halyards were as thick as my wrist and the cone was frozen to the mast.

I spent the morning tapping ice off the rigging with a wooden mallet, while Jory held the ladder and offered advice. Twigs tinkled like teaspoons. Mrs Furze awarded no points and slid most of the way home. The score stands at five to four.

volumes.title: A Gale in the Night
volumes.text:
February at Skerry Point. Jory Pike was in bed with a cold, wrapped in three jerseys, and sent word by his granddaughter that the weather would hold. He could not smell anything at all, which I suspect was the trouble.

I am Maren Coldwick, and I keep the signal mast and the barometer. At dusk the glass was dropping so quickly that I could see the difference between one tapping and the next. I hoisted the cone by lantern light and went along the quay knocking on doors.

The gale arrived at midnight, shrieked for four hours, and left before breakfast. It was short and sharp, as fast-falling storms are. A dinghy was found in the churchyard, unharmed. Mrs Furze brought the wager book to Jory's bedside. Five all. He said it was unsporting to hold a storm while a man had no nose. I took him soup anyway.

volumes.title: Hail on the Quay
volumes.text:
March, and the tenth storm of the wager between my barometer and Jory Pike. I am Maren Coldwick of the signal station at Skerry Point, and I lost this one fairly.

It was a morning of sunshine and sharp showers. Jory, recovered from his cold, studied a line of tall clouds out to sea, white on top and dark as slate beneath, all leaning the same way. Squall by noon, he said, and hail in it. My glass showed nothing worth a cone.

It struck at ten to twelve: a wall of wind, one crack of thunder, and hailstones the size of dried peas that drummed on the upturned boats and gathered in the gutters like spilled sugar. Only as it hit did the barometer give a little startled jump. A squall is too small and quick for it. Jory six, glass five, and two weeks to go.

volumes.title: Gulls on the Water
volumes.text:
I am Maren Coldwick, signal-keeper at Skerry Point, and with spring a fortnight off my barometer stood one point behind Jory Pike in our season's wager.

On the twentieth of March the glass began to fall. Jory would not have it. The gulls were riding the swell beyond the bar, he said, and the sky was clean. I showed him the brass pointer. He showed me the gulls. We stood on the quay disagreeing until Mrs Furze, our judge, told us both to go home.

I hoisted the cone on the strength of the glass alone, and felt lonely doing it. The wind got up after dark and blew a full gale from the west until morning. No boat was out. Six all. Jory came up the path at first light to say so himself, which I thought handsome of him. The glass, I noticed, had not risen again.

volumes.title: The Great Blow
volumes.text:
The last storm of the season at Skerry Point was the worst, and nobody could have missed it. My barometer sank lower than I, Maren Coldwick, had ever seen it, off the bottom of the printed scale. At the same hour Jory Pike arrived breathless to report gulls walking up the village street, inland, in single file.

We hoisted the cone together, and the drum beneath it, which means stay in and mean it. It blew for two days. The sea came over the wall and into the net loft. When it cleared, all eleven boats were afloat and every soul was at home.

Mrs Furze closed the wager book: seven all, a draw. So Jory and I painted the signal mast together, he holding the ladder, and split one herring supper. I read the glass first now. Then I ask Jory.

volumes.title: The Clerk of Frosts
volumes.text:
I am Wilmot Garrick, sixteen, and since September I have been bound apprentice to Mistress Edda Thornlow, Frost Clerk of the Lowlands. Her cottage at Hollow Ash holds forty ledgers, one for each winter she has watched. Every orchard and market garden between here and Emberwick plants by them.

The tables are simple to look at. For each year: the date of the first frost, the date of the last, and the count of frost nights between. The work behind them is a reading at dawn and another at dusk, every day.

She showed me the instruments. One thermometer hangs in a white slatted box at the height of my chin, to take the air. Another lies on two pegs just above the grass. They will disagree, she said, and when you understand why, you may hold the pen. Until then I carry the lantern and rule the lines.

volumes.title: Frost on the Grass
volumes.text:
The first entry of year forty-one in the Frost Tables was made on the third of October, and I, Wilmot Garrick, apprentice, very nearly missed it.

At dawn the thermometer in the white box at Hollow Ash stood four degrees above freezing. No frost, I called. Mistress Thornlow, the Frost Clerk, sent me back out to read the one lying over the grass. It showed two degrees below. My boots left dark green prints across the stiff lawn.

This is a ground frost. On a clear, still night the earth gives up its warmth to the sky, and the coldest air lies in a skin against the grass, while a few feet higher it stays mild. Beans feel it. Apple boughs do not. She entered it in the ground column. Two columns, she said, because a strawberry and a plum live at different heights.

volumes.title: Dipper's Bottom
volumes.text:
On the nineteenth of October the air thermometer at Hollow Ash touched freezing, and the dahlias by the cottage gate turned black in a night. First air frost, year forty-one. Mistress Thornlow, Frost Clerk of the Lowlands, entered it; I, her apprentice Wilmot Garrick, ruled the line.

Then she walked me down to Dipper's Bottom, the dip in the low field, carrying a third thermometer. It read five degrees colder than the garden, two hundred paces away.

Cold air is heavy, she explained. On a still night it runs downhill like water and gathers in the hollows, and a hedge across a slope will dam it into a pool. That is why old orchards stand on the hillsides and never in the bottoms. I stood in the hollow and felt the cold lying around my ankles. I had thought all of a field was one weather.

volumes.title: Hoar on the Gatepost
volumes.text:
November at Hollow Ash in the Lowlands, and my third month as apprentice to the Frost Clerk. This morning every gate, thistle and spider's web was furred with white, and Mistress Thornlow handed me her reading glass before I had my coat buttoned.

Hoar frost is not frozen dew. It grows. The moisture in the air settles straight onto anything cold as ice, crystal upon crystal, into feathers and needles and tiny fern fronds. Through the glass, a fence rail was a forest.

It needs three things, and she made me, Wilmot Garrick, recite them: a clear sky, still air, and a long night. Cloud is a blanket; under cloud the ground keeps its warmth. Wind stirs the cold skin away. I measured the longest needles on the gatepost at half an inch and entered the figure in the remarks column myself. My first ink in the tables.

volumes.title: Rime on the Windward Side
volumes.text:
I am Wilmot Garrick, apprentice to Mistress Edda Thornlow, who keeps the Frost Tables for the Lowlands. In December a freezing fog sat over Hollow Ash for three days, and I learned that I had been using one word for two things.

The white that grew on the hedges was not hoar. Hoar comes on clear nights and coats a twig evenly, all round. This was rime: the fog's own droplets, blown against cold wood and frozen where they struck. It builds only on the side the wind comes from, in rough white combs, each tooth pointing into the breeze.

So you can read the wind after it has gone, she said, and had me walk the lane with a compass. Every comb pointed north-east. By the third day they were as long as my finger. Rime, north-east, three days, I wrote, and she let the entry stand.

volumes.title: Ferns on the Glass
volumes.text:
Midwinter at Hollow Ash, the Frost Clerk's cottage in the Lowlands. I woke to find my attic window grown over with white ferns, and spent a quarter of an hour admiring them before I, Wilmot Garrick, remembered the dawn reading.

Mistress Thornlow says window frost is the warm, damp breath of the house freezing on cold glass, and that it follows the scratches and specks of dust. A clean pane grows plainer ferns. I have not cleaned mine.

This is the season when the letters come. A nurseryman at Emberwick asks how late he has ever dared set out his beans. A widow with six plum trees asks which wall is safest. She answers each from the forty ledgers and I copy the replies fair. The tables, I begin to see, are forty years of somebody getting up early on behalf of strangers.

volumes.title: Bearing Ice
volumes.text:
January brought eleven frost nights running to Hollow Ash, and Mistress Thornlow, the Frost Clerk, sent me out with an auger. I am her apprentice, Wilmot Garrick, and the tables have a column I had not noticed: ice on the mill pond.

I bored through at the same post each morning. One inch, then two, then three and a half. She will not let the village children skate until it reaches four, clear and dark; white, bubbled ice counts for half. On the day it passed, she hung a blue rag on the pond gate, and by noon the whole school was out.

The frost goes down into the soil as well. I dug in the bean plot and found the ground hard as brick for the depth of my hand. Beneath that the earth was soft, and a worm was curled up there, waiting it out.

volumes.title: The Black Frost
volumes.text:
I am Wilmot Garrick, apprentice at Hollow Ash, where the Frost Tables of the Lowlands are kept. In February Mistress Thornlow took a cough, and for nine mornings I read the thermometers alone and carried the figures up to her on a slate.

On the fourth morning I thought the instruments had broken. The air stood eight degrees below freezing, and there was no frost to be seen. No white on the grass, none on the gate. The fields were dark and dry, and a thin wind came steadily from the east.

That is a black frost, she said from her pillows. The air is too dry to make crystals, so the cold arrives with nothing to show for itself. It is the kind that splits bark and kills the winter greens. Never trust your eyes over the glass. I entered it myself in my best hand.

volumes.title: The Ground Heaves
volumes.text:
March at Hollow Ash in the Lowlands: thaw by day, frost by night, and the Frost Clerk on her feet again. Mistress Thornlow set me, Wilmot Garrick, her apprentice, to walk the garden each morning and write down what had moved.

A good deal had. Wet soil swells as it freezes. Night after night it lifts whatever sits in it, and by day it sinks back, but never quite to where it began. The autumn-sown onions were standing on their roots like stilts. The gatepost leaned a thumb's width further than in February.

In the bare bed by the well I found the cause in miniature: bundles of fine ice needles, an inch tall, each carrying a crumb of earth on its tip like a hat. I pressed the onions back with my heel, as she showed me. The tables have a remarks column for all of this.

volumes.title: Blossom and the White Flag
volumes.text:
April. The plum orchards of the Lowlands are in flower, and at Hollow Ash the Frost Tables have become the most important books in the district. I am Wilmot Garrick, apprentice to the Frost Clerk, and I now understand what the winter was practice for.

A frost in January harms nobody. A frost on open blossom takes the year's fruit in a night. In forty years, Mistress Thornlow's tables show, the last frost has fallen as early as the ninth of April and as late as the twenty-second of May.

So each evening we judge the night ahead, and if we fear frost I run a white flag up the pole on the cottage roof. It can be seen from five farms, and they pass the word on. I have raised it twice this month. Both times she decided. Next time, she says, I shall.

volumes.title: The Night of the Fourteenth
volumes.text:
On the evening of the thirteenth of May the sky over Hollow Ash cleared from the north, and the wind dropped to nothing. Mistress Thornlow, Frost Clerk of the Lowlands, sat down in her chair and looked at me. I am Wilmot Garrick, her apprentice. The decision was mine.

I went through it as she taught me. Clear sky: no blanket. Still air: nothing to stir the cold away. At sunset the thermometer was already falling a degree every half hour, and the grass was dry. Frost by three in the morning, I said, and hard in the hollows. I ran up the white flag.

Lanterns moved in the orchards all night. The growers lit heaps of damp straw between the rows so that smoke lay over the blossom like a quilt. At dawn the thermometer over the grass read three below. Most of the plums were saved.

volumes.title: The Line under the Year
volumes.text:
The frost of the fourteenth of May was the last. We waited three weeks to be sure, as the rule requires, and on a warm June morning at Hollow Ash Mistress Edda Thornlow opened the Frost Tables at year forty-one and held out the pen to me, Wilmot Garrick, her apprentice.

I wrote the summary. First ground frost, the third of October. First air frost, the nineteenth of October. Last frost, the fourteenth of May. Frost nights, fifty-eight. Remarks: one black frost; white flag raised three times; the plums of the Lowlands mostly saved.

Then I ruled a line under the year, and she had me put my initials beside hers, small, in the corner. The thermometers will disagree again in autumn, and I know why now. She has ordered a new ledger from the binder in Emberwick. There is room on the shelf for forty more.

volumes.title: The Fellman
volumes.text:
I am Linnet Garrow, journeyman letter-cutter, and I came to Emberwick this spring a stranger. The town council has given me a round slab of fell slate, to be set in the market square. On it I am to cut a wind-rose with twelve points, and at each point the name of the wind that blows from it. The true name, the clerk said. Whatever people actually call it.

Nobody in the council chamber could tell me more than four. So I am to walk the district and ask.

I began with the north, at a shepherd's hut below Harrow Fell. They call the north wind the Fellman there. It comes down off the tops cold, dry and clear, and you can see every wall for ten miles when it blows. A good drying wind, the shepherd said, and a liar about how warm the sun is.

volumes.title: The Whittler
volumes.text:
The second point of my wind-rose lies a little east of north. I am Linnet Garrow, letter-cutter, collecting the names of the twelve winds for a slate that will lie in Emberwick market square, and for this one I climbed to the slate quarry at Cold Rigg in the Northern Fells.

The quarrymen call it the Whittler. It is a thin wind, they say, never strong, that finds the gap between cuff and glove and pares a man down a shaving at a time. It blows into April and brings small hard snow that rattles like rice.

I felt it myself. It came round the corner of the cutting shed and went straight through two coats. The foreman's wife gave me a hot stone for my pocket and spelled the name for me, though she had never seen it written. Two names in the notebook. Ten to find.

volumes.title: The Dry Aunt
volumes.text:
East by north of Emberwick the land flattens toward the Lowlands, and there, at a farm called Stonecrop, I found the third wind for my rose. I am Linnet Garrow, letter-cutter, hired by the town to carve the names of the twelve winds as local people say them.

The farmer's mother called this one the Dry Aunt, and would not explain until I had drunk a cup of tea. It comes in spring, she said. It brings no rain. It cracks lips, lifts the seed bed off in dust and puts everyone out of temper, and yet the washing dries in an hour and you cannot fault its housekeeping. Just like an aunt of hers.

Back in Emberwick, in Dunstan Crake's yard, where the slab lies on trestles, I cut the first three names. The slate is sound and takes a clean edge.

volumes.title: The Miller's Friend
volumes.text:
Due east of Emberwick the Lowlands are dotted with windmills, and I supposed the millers would have a name for the east wind. They did. I am Linnet Garrow, letter-cutter, a third of the way round the wind-rose I am making for the market square.

At Tolley's Mill they call it the Miller's Friend. It is not a strong wind, but it is the steadiest of the twelve. It will blow from one quarter from Monday to Saturday, and he can set his sails once and grind the whole week without touching them. Gusty winds break gear. This one pays the rent.

He let me stand on the gallery while the sails went round, each one passing with a soft whoop. Up there I noticed the weathercock had worn a bright groove in its spindle, facing east. I wrote the name on a flour bag.

volumes.title: The Chaff-Wind
volumes.text:
I am Linnet Garrow, cutting a twelve-point wind-rose in slate for Emberwick and walking the country to learn what each wind is called. The fifth point lies south of east, and I reached it at harvest, on the threshing floor of a farm near Barley Cross.

There they wait for the Chaff-Wind. It is a warm, light, dry breeze of late summer afternoons. The women toss the threshed grain up from baskets; the heavy corn falls back, and the wind carries the husks off in a golden smoke. Too little wind and the chaff falls with the grain. Too much and the grain goes over the hedge.

They put a basket in my hands. I was bad at it and was laughed at kindly. I had chaff in my hair for two days, and found some in the groove of the letter C when I cut it.

volumes.title: The Honey Wind
volumes.text:
A little east of south from Emberwick lie the orchards and bee gardens of Hollow Ash. I went there in September for the sixth name on my wind-rose. I am Linnet Garrow, the letter-cutter carving the twelve winds in slate for the market square.

An old beekeeper named Aldith told me this one without being asked. The Honey Wind, she said: soft and warm, coming in May and June when the blossom is open. Her bees fly straight up it to the clover as if along a string, and on a Honey Wind day a hive can gain two pounds.

I was too late in the year to meet it, so she sat me among the hives and described it. I notice that the cold winds are named for what they do to people, and the warm ones for what they bring. Six names. Half the rose.

volumes.title: Mother Mild
volumes.text:
Due south. I am Linnet Garrow, letter-cutter, more than half way round the twelve winds whose names I am to carve for Emberwick, and for the south wind I had only to ask a washerwoman at the Ember bridge, who answered as though I had asked the name of her own sister.

Mother Mild. It is the wind that ends a frost. It comes up from the south wet and warm, and in the morning the icicles are dripping, the snow has gone grey and soft, and the lanes are running. It rarely blows hard. It simply leans on the cold until the cold gives way.

It brings low cloud and fine rain, she said, and chilblains ease, and old dogs come out to lie on the step. I cut the name that week in Dunstan Crake's yard, with the first fog of autumn beading on the slate.

volumes.title: The Marsh Breath
volumes.text:
South-south-west of Emberwick the river Ember loses itself in the marsh, and the wind from that quarter is known in the town by its smell before anything else. I am Linnet Garrow; I am collecting the local names of the twelve winds to cut in a slate wind-rose; and this was the eighth.

The reed cutters call it the Marsh Breath. It is slow and damp and comes mostly at dusk in autumn, smelling of mud, mint and wet reed. It carries the mist inland with it, a field at a time, so that the marsh seems to be walking into town.

A reed cutter named Hob poled me out in his flat boat to feel it rise. The reeds bowed toward Emberwick all together, and my hair went limp. Bad for bread and fiddle strings, he said, good for eels. Eight names. The slab is two-thirds lettered.

volumes.title: The Wet Shepherd
volumes.text:
I am Linnet Garrow, letter-cutter, and in November I walked out to the Grey Coast to ask after the last winds for the rose I am carving for Emberwick market square. The ninth point lies between south-west and west. At Skerry Point they knew it at once.

The Wet Shepherd, said the net-menders. It blows for days on end from over the sea, mild and strong, and it drives the rain clouds inland ahead of it in long grey flocks, with hardly a gap to dry a shirt in. Most of the district's rain comes on it. The farmers bless it in a dry summer and nobody blesses it in November.

I stood on the harbour wall and watched three flocks go over inside an hour, each trailing its skirt of rain across the water. Then I walked back very wet, with the name safe inside my hat.

volumes.title: The Greyback
volumes.text:
The west wind on the Grey Coast is the one they speak of quietly. I am Linnet Garrow, letter-cutter, tenth name into a wind-rose of twelve for the town of Emberwick, and I heard this one from the signal-keeper at Skerry Point, beside a mast with a black cone flying.

The Greyback. It is the gale wind, straight off the open sea, and it takes its name from the long grey waves it sends in, each with a back like a whale. When the Greyback blows, the boats stay on their moorings and the spray goes over the harbour wall.

I saw it do so. I spent the afternoon in the net loft with the crews, who mended and told stories and listened to the roof. A name like that should be cut deep, one of them said. I have given it letters a shade deeper than the rest.

volumes.title: Salt Tom
volumes.text:
After the gale came the eleventh wind, as it always does. I am Linnet Garrow, the letter-cutter collecting the names of the twelve winds for Emberwick's market square, and I was still on the Grey Coast when the weather turned.

The wind swung round north of west and the sky broke open. Now it was all bright blue gaps and sudden hard showers, sun and hail inside the same quarter hour, and the gulls were flung about like scraps of paper. The children at Skerry Point call this wind Salt Tom. He is cold and rough, but he is playing. He steals caps. He leaves salt on the windows three miles inland.

They held a contest to see whose cap went furthest. Eleven names. But when I asked anyone about the last point, north by west, they shook their heads. That one does not come here, they said.

volumes.title: The Keyhole Wind
volumes.text:
I came back to Emberwick in December with eleven winds and one blank point, north by west. I am Linnet Garrow, letter-cutter. Shepherds, millers, beekeepers and fishermen had each named the wind that mattered to them, and none of them knew the twelfth.

I confessed as much to Dunstan Crake beside the nearly finished rose. He laughed until he had to sit down. That one is ours, he said. It blows down Tallow Lane on winter evenings and whistles in every lock in town. It is the Keyhole Wind.

I had walked the whole district and never asked at home. I cut the name that night with the wind itself fluting in the yard door. The rose was set in the square on the shortest day. People stand on it and turn to face whatever is blowing, and say its name, and I am no longer a stranger here.
